material_units.source_text: Worked example (an excursion with an atom). Let $X\sim\mathcal U(-1,1)$ be the signed distance of the state beyond a constraint boundary (positive means violated) and $Z=\max(X,0)=X^+$ the excursion. Then $\mathbb P(Z=0)=\mathbb P(X\le0)=\tfrac12$: an atom at zero. For $0\le z\le1$, $F_Z(z)=\mathbb P(X\le z)=(1+z)/2$, so $F_Z$ jumps from $0$ to $\tfrac12$ at $z=0$ and then rises linearly to $1$ (figure). A nondegenerate Gaussian has no atoms and assigns positive probability to negative values; a degenerate Gaussian is a single point mass. Neither represents this mixed law.

For the excursion above, $\mathbb E[Z]=0\cdot\tfrac12+\int_0^1z\cdot\tfrac12\,dz=\tfrac14$: the atom contributes nothing, the density $\tfrac12$ on $(0,1]$ the rest. Counting violations: with $c_t=\mathbf 1\{x_t\gt1\}$ and $N=\sum_{t=1}^Tc_t$, linearity gives $\mathbb E[N]=\sum_t\mathbb P(x_t\gt1)$ even though the states of one episode are dependent. If each of $T=50$ steps violates with probability $0.004$, then $\mathbb E[N]=0.2$. Since $N$ is a nonnegative integer, $\mathbf 1\{N\ge1\}\le N$, hence $\mathbb P(\text{at least one violation})\le\mathbb E[N]=0.2$ whatever the dependence. A Boolean test becomes a signed monitor by subtracting one half: $\mathbf 1\{\text{test passed}\}-\tfrac12\in\{-\tfrac12,+\tfrac12\}$ is positive exactly when the test passes.
